body:
MYK'S NEXT PRIORITY, raised 2026-08-04 after driving the admin page by hand. His framing: "like a
file system sort of."

THE MODEL, as he stated it. Given the root ground, containers A and B, and A.1 and A.2 inside A: A.2
with `inherit` set gathers anything in the ROOT GROUND or in A, and NOT anything in B or A.1.

So inheritance follows the ANCESTOR CHAIN — the path from the root down to this container — never the
whole tree. A container sees what is above it on its own path. It does not see siblings, and it does not
see its own descendants. That is lexical scope, and it is the filesystem intuition he named: what is on
your path, not what is in someone else's branch.

DIRECTION IS THE WHOLE POINT, AND THIS DOES NOT REVERSE §39.3(a). A builder who reads that section
first will think it does, so say it plainly:
  - §39.3(a) settled that a parent does NOT auto-gather its CHILDREN. Upward merge was refused because
    it would destroy the per-container divergence story (a negation admitted to `alice.folklore` must
    not bind in every wider read).
  - `inherit` is the OPPOSITE direction: a child gathers its ANCESTORS.
The two compose without conflict. Downward-invisible, upward-visible. Both remain true.

THE TRAVERSAL IS NEW, and it must not be confused with the one that exists. `subtreeOf`
(`src/server/admin.ts:177`) walks DOWNWARD through `parent` and `inboxOf` edges to answer AUTHORIZATION
reach — "which containers may this user touch". `inherit` needs an ANCESTOR walk to answer GATHER
membership — "what does this container contain". Different question, opposite direction, and reusing
either for the other is a bug waiting to happen. Containment is a tree (§28.8), so an ancestor walk
terminates; the cycle check at `container.ts:340` already guards the graph.

WHY A KNOB RATHER THAN A TERM. A child's membership Term could restate its parent's clauses today, but
that is copy-paste which drifts the moment the parent's Term changes, and it cannot reach a
SEPARATE-posture ancestor at all (that pool is not in the primary ground a Term selects over). A knob is
declarative and stays correct as ancestors change. That is the case for building it rather than
documenting a recipe.

THE DESIGN QUESTIONS. Several are Myk's; the ticket does not decide them.

(a) IS THE KNOB IMMUTABLE? `trust` and `posture` already are, per §28.4 (`container.ts:321`: "a
    different trust posture is a NEW container"). Inheritance changes what a container CONTAINS, so
    flipping it later retroactively changes what every past read would have resolved. LEAN: immutable,
    for the same reason posture is — but this is a real decision with a migration consequence.

(b) DOES INHERITANCE CARRY NEGATIONS? IT MUST — this is the H1 hazard and the heart of the rails. If A
    holds D1 and also holds D2 negating D1, then an inheriting A.2 must gather BOTH. Gathering D1 while
    dropping the admitted D2 is precisely the strand §39.2 warns about, and it would make an inheriting
    child show a claim its own parent has retracted.

(c) CAN A CHILD INHERIT THROUGH A SEPARATE-POSTURE ANCESTOR? That pool is not in the primary ground. It
    must either refuse the declaration outright or require the pool ATTACHED at read time — and per H9
    it must never resolve as if the ancestor were empty. `containerScope` already has exactly this
    refusal for unattached pools; reuse it rather than inventing a second answer.

(d) DOES INHERITANCE INCLUDE AN ANCESTOR'S INBOX POOLS? A container's members include the inboxes spawned
    for its connections (§39.3d). So an inheriting child would see what a connection wrote to its parent.
    Probably right for consistency, and it must be stated either way rather than discovered.

(e) INHERITANCE IS BY REFERENCE, NEVER BY COPY. It resolves at gather time. So erasing a delta from A
    removes it from A.2's view with no second sweep, and erasure keeps its full guarantee. Make this a
    CRITERION, so no later optimization turns it into a copy and silently creates a second place a
    forgotten delta survives.

(f) IT WIDENS WHAT A CONNECTION CAN READ, AND THE CONSENT PAGE MUST SAY SO. This is the security-relevant
    consequence. §39 binds a connection to one container and the consent page names it. If that container
    INHERITS, the connection also reads everything up its path — including the root ground. A consent page
    that names `alice:folklore` while the connection can read all of `alice` and the store's root is
    FALSE, and falsehood in a consent dialogue is the H7 shape where it does most damage. Either the
    consent copy states the inherited reach, or a connection-bound container is refused the knob. MYK'S
    CALL, and it should be made before any code.

RAILS, two-sided everywhere, at both levels:
  - A.2 with `inherit` gathers a delta from the root ground and a delta from A — asserted at the delta
    level (it is in the gather) AND the object level (a View through a Schema resolves it).
  - The SAME read does NOT contain B's delta or A.1's delta. Named live bystanders, so the rail can see
    over-inheriting as well as under-inheriting.
  - A.2 WITHOUT the knob sees neither — the knob is what does the work, and a rail that omits this
    passes with the feature deleted.
  - The negation case from (b): A holds D1 and D2-negating-D1; A.2's View resolves without D1.
  - The separate-ancestor case from (c): refused, or refused-when-unattached, with the H9 message.

MIGRATION: adding a knob to the container declaration changes the bytes of that delta kind. Per the §20
corollary the new shape must be unambiguously distinguishable from every prior spelling, and the PR owes
a `src/migrate/` step in the SAME change. An absent knob must read as "does not inherit" so every
existing container keeps its current contents exactly.

DESIGN-STAGE. The deliverable is a working spec with every criterion naming its verification, then STOP
for Myk. It amends §28 (containers); P1 decides whether it earns its own section number. The landing PR
is his merge — it changes what the system promises, and (f) touches the consent surface.
title: A container inherits its ancestors' deltas — the `inherit` knob, a path not a tree
